topic: A normal TSH on thyroid medicine means the dose fits, not that you can stop
angle: Clients often ask to stop levothyroxine once the report is normal. A normal TSH on dose means the dose suits the body now; treatment is usually long term and the dose changes over life (weight, age, other medicines, iron/calcium absorption), so keep retesting and discuss dose only with the prescribing doctor. Client example C02 (TSH into range on an unchanged dose; CRP did not improve).
hook: When a thyroid report comes back normal, several of my clients ask me the same thing: can I stop the tablet now?
draft:
When a thyroid report finally comes back normal, several of my clients ask me the same thing. Can I stop the tablet now?

I understand why. Nobody wants to take a pill every morning for the rest of their life.

Here's how I explain it, using one client's numbers.

She came to me with a TSH above 5 and very low B12, on a small daily dose of thyroid medicine. Over six months we worked on B12, iron, protein and strength training. By the end, her TSH was under 2. Her dose hadn't changed.

That's a good result. It means the dose now suits her body. It doesn't mean her thyroid can manage without the tablet. The tablet is part of the reason the number looks good.

Thyroid medicine replaces a hormone your gland isn't making enough of. A 2019 review in Advances in Therapy says most people with hypothyroidism take it for a long time, usually for the rest of their life. What changes over the years is the dose. Weight, age, other medicines, and iron or calcium supplements can all shift how much you need.

So a normal report is a reason to keep retesting: a few months after any dose change, then about once a year once things are steady. If you want to talk about your dose, have that conversation with the doctor who prescribed it.

One honest note on her case: not everything improved. Her inflammation marker didn't come down, and it became the main thing left to address.

If you're on thyroid medicine, when was your TSH last checked?

#ThyroidHealth #Hypothyroidism
final:
When a thyroid report comes back normal, several of my clients ask me the same thing: can I stop the tablet now?

I understand the question. Nobody wants to take a pill every morning for the rest of their life.

One client's numbers explain my answer well. She came to me on a small daily dose of thyroid medicine, with a TSH above 5 and very low B12. Over six months we worked on B12, iron, protein and strength training. By the end her TSH was under 2, and she was on the same dose she started with.

I was happy with that. What it tells me is that her dose now suits her body. It doesn't tell me her thyroid could manage without the tablet, because the tablet is part of why that number looks good.

Thyroid medicine replaces a hormone the gland is short of. A 2019 review in Advances in Therapy says people with hypothyroidism usually take it for a long time, typically for the rest of their life. The dose is what tends to change. Body weight, age and some other medicines can shift how much you need, and iron or calcium supplements can reduce how much of the tablet you absorb.

So a normal report means you keep retesting: a few months after any dose change, then about once a year when things are steady. If you want to talk about your dose, have that conversation with the doctor who prescribed it.

Not everything improved for her, by the way. Her inflammation marker didn't come down, and that became the main thing left to work on.

If you're on thyroid medicine, when was your TSH last checked?

#ThyroidHealth #Hypothyroidism
